claim: Layer II of the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) contains two principal cell types: pyramidal cells and stellate cells.
source: Layer II of the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) contains two principal cell types: pyramidal cells and stellate cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is established scientific knowledge about MEC anatomy.

claim: Stellate cells express reelin.
source: Stellate cells express reelin (Pesold et al., 1998; Kitamura et al., 2014; Fuchs et al., 2016; Winterer et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Stellate cells have large sag potentials.
source: Stellate cells express reelin (Pesold et al., 1998; Kitamura et al., 2014; Fuchs et al., 2016; Winterer et al., 2017), have large sag potentials (Dickson et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dickson et al., 2000.

claim: Stellate cells have superficially branching dendrites.
source: superficially branching dendrites (Canto and Witter, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Canto and Witter, 2012.

claim: Stellate cells in rodents have sub-threshold membrane potential oscillations in the theta range.
source: and, at least in rodents, sub-threshold membrane potential oscillations in the theta range (Alonso and Llinás, 1989)
evidence: Supported by citation to Alonso and Llinás, 1989.

claim: Pyramidal cells form tight clusters.
source: Pyramidal cells form tight clusters (Kitamura et al., 2014; Ray et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kitamura et al., 2014 and Ray et al., 2014.

claim: Pyramidal cells express calbindin and WFS-1.
source: express calbindin and WFS-1 (Kitamura et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kitamura et al., 2014.

claim: Pyramidal cells have thick apical dendrites.
source: have thick apical dendrites (Canto and Witter, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Canto and Witter, 2012.

claim: Pyramidal cells receive strong cholinergic input from the medial septum.
source: and receive strong cholinergic input from the medial septum (Ray et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ray et al., 2014.

claim: Pyramidal cells are connected via 5-HT 3a positive interneurons.
source: pyramidal cells are connected via 5-HT 3a positive interneurons (Fuchs et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fuchs et al., 2016.

claim: Stellate cells are connected via fast-spiking parvalbumin (PV+) cells and slower spiking somatostatin-positive cells.
source: while stellate cells are connected via fast-spiking parvalbumin (PV+) cells and slower spiking somatostatin-positive cells (Fuchs et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fuchs et al., 2016.

claim: Up to 14% of pyramidal cells project to stellate cells.
source: it has been estimated that up to 14% of pyramidal cells project to stellate cells (Winterer et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Winterer et al., 2017.

claim: Some cells express an intermediate stellate/pyramidal identity.
source: and some cells express an intermediate stellate/pyramidal identity (Fuchs et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fuchs et al., 2016.

claim: Nearly every stellate cell projects to the DG, CA3 and/or CA2 regions of the hippocampus.
source: Nearly every stellate cell projects to the DG, CA3 and/or CA2 regions of the hippocampus, where terminals from stellate cells make up the main, and nearly exclusive, excitatory input from the MEC (Kitamura et al., 2014; Ray et al., 2014; Varga et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kitamura et al., 2014; Ray et al., 2014; Varga et al., 2010.

claim: Terminals from stellate cells make up the main, and nearly exclusive, excitatory input from the MEC to DG, CA3, and CA2.
source: Nearly every stellate cell projects to the DG, CA3 and/or CA2 regions of the hippocampus, where terminals from stellate cells make up the main, and nearly exclusive, excitatory input from the MEC (Kitamura et al., 2014; Ray et al., 2014; Varga et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kitamura et al., 2014; Ray et al., 2014; Varga et al., 2010.

claim: A subset of layer II pyramidal cells project to the CA1 region.
source: A subset of the cells project to the CA1 region (Kitamura et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kitamura et al., 2014.

claim: A subset of layer II pyramidal cells project to the contralateral hemisphere of the MEC.
source: and to the contralateral hemisphere of the MEC (Varga et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Varga et al., 2010.

claim: Layer II pyramidal cells do not terminate in the DG, CA3 or CA2 regions.
source: but importantly, they do not terminate in the DG, CA3 or CA2 regions (Kitamura et al., 2014; Ray et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kitamura et al., 2014 and Ray et al., 2014.

claim: Intracellular recordings of stellate and pyramidal cells in mice running on a virtual linear track have shown that both types could be putative grid cells.
source: Intracellular recordings of stellate and pyramidal cells in mice running on a virtual linear track have shown that both types could be putative grid cells (Domnisoru et al., 2013; Schmidt-Hieber and Häusser, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Domnisoru et al., 2013 and Schmidt-Hieber and Häusser, 2013.

claim: Imaging studies of freely moving animals have found that both stellate and pyramidal cells could be putative grid cells.
source: and imaging studies of freely moving animals have found the same (Sun et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2015.

claim: Only 3 of 94 putative stellate cells (near chance levels) were grid cells based on theta phase locking classification.
source: Based on this classifier, only 3 of 94 putative stellate cells (near chance levels) were grid cells (Tang et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tang et al., 2014.

claim: The 'EC-tTA' line expresses almost exclusively in the parahippocampal region (entorhinal cortex together with the pre- and para- subiculum).
source: To gain genetic access to stellate cells, we used the 'EC-tTA' line (Yasuda and Mayford, 2006) that expresses almost exclusively in the parahippocampal region (entorhinal cortex together with the pre- and para- subiculum).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yasuda and Mayford, 2006.

claim: Within the MEC, the expression of the 'EC-tTA' line is confined to layer II.
source: Within the MEC, where we targeted our tetrodes, the expression is confined to layer II (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1 showing expression pattern.

claim: The transgene-expressing cells in layer II of the MEC in the 'EC-tTA' line have stellate-like morphologies.
source: Previous work on the 'EC-tTA' line has shown that the transgene-expressing cells in layer II of the MEC have stellate-like morphologies, project to the dentate gyrus and CA3 regions of the hippocampus (Rowland et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rowland et al., 2013.

claim: The transgene-expressing cells in the 'EC-tTA' line project to the dentate gyrus and CA3 regions of the hippocampus.
source: Previous work on the 'EC-tTA' line has shown that the transgene-expressing cells in layer II of the MEC have stellate-like morphologies, project to the dentate gyrus and CA3 regions of the hippocampus (Rowland et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Rowland et al., 2013.

claim: The 'EC-tTA' line often shows distinctive circular gaps in expression.
source: and often show distinctive circular gaps in expression (Kanter et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanter et al., 2017.

claim: The circular gaps in expression presumably correlate with circular clusters of calbindin-positive pyramidal cells.
source: which presumably correlate with circular clusters of calbindin-positive pyramidal cells (Kitamura et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citation to Kitamura et al., 2014.

claim: Only 3 of 303 Arch-expressing cells expressed calbindin (~1%).
source: Overall, only a small minority of the Arch-expressing MEC cells expressed calbindin (3 of 303 Arch-expressing cells expressed calbindin, ~ 1%; 3 of 433 calbindin expressing cells expressed Arch, less than 1%)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization and antibody staining.

claim: 97.2% of Arch-expressing cells expressed reelin (315 of 324 ArchT-expressing cells expressed reelin).
source: while 97.2% expressed reelin (315 of 324 ArchT-expressing cells expressed reelin; 315 of 967 of reelin expressing cells expressed ArchT, 32.5%; Figure 1C,D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: 32.5% of reelin expressing cells expressed ArchT (315 of 967 of reelin expressing cells expressed ArchT).
source: while 97.2% expressed reelin (315 of 324 ArchT-expressing cells expressed reelin; 315 of 967 of reelin expressing cells expressed ArchT, 32.5%; Figure 1C,D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Arch-expressing cells avoided clusters of calbindin-positive cells.
source: Arch-expressing cells avoided clusters of calbindin-positive cells (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by visual evidence in Figure 1B.

claim: ArchT expression overlapped extremely well with reelin.
source: but overlapped extremely well with reelin (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by visual evidence in Figure 1D.

claim: GFP-labeled fibers were found in the molecular layer of the dentate gyrus and CA3.
source: Finally, to confirm that the ArchT-expressing cells project to the hippocampus, we checked for GFP-labeled fibers in the molecular layer of the dentate gyrus and CA3, the expected termination zones of MEC stellate cells, and found intense labeling in these areas (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The EC-tTA x tetO-ArchT-GFP cross drives expression of ArchT almost exclusively in stellate cells in MECII.
source: The cross therefore drives expression of ArchT almost exclusively in stellate cells in MECII.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on overlap between ArchT and reelin/calbindin.

claim: 75 cells were tagged from a population of 578 (~13% tagged cells).
source: We applied a latency threshold of 5 ms, which eliminated three outlier cells and left a total of 75 tagged cells from a population of 578 (~13% tagged cells).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from optogenetic tagging.

claim: Most of the tagged cells had near-zero millisecond latencies (median latency = 0.85 ms).
source: Most of the cells had near-zero millisecond latencies (median latency = 0.85 ms, Figure 2C–E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: 25.3% of tagged cells were grid cells (16% pure, 9.3% mixed).
source: The tagged population included grid cells (25.3%; 16% pure, 9.3% mixed)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from functional classification of tagged cells.

claim: 12% of tagged cells were head direction cells (9.3% pure, 2.7% mixed).
source: head direction cells (12%; 9.3% pure, 2.7% mixed)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from functional classification of tagged cells.

claim: 16% of tagged cells were speed cells (8% pure, 8% mixed).
source: speed cells (16%; 8% pure, 8% mixed)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from functional classification of tagged cells.

claim: 1.3% of tagged cells were border cells (1.3% pure, 0% mixed).
source: border cells (1.3%; 1.3% pure, 0% mixed)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from functional classification of tagged cells.

claim: 56.0% of tagged cells were unclassified.
source: and unclassified cells (56.0%)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from functional classification of tagged cells.

claim: 35.6% of untagged cells were grid cells (26.8% pure, 8.8% mixed).
source: The untagged population included grid cells (35.6%; 26.8% pure, 8.8% mixed)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from functional classification of untagged cells.

claim: 9.1% of untagged cells were head direction cells (6.1% pure, 3% mixed).
source: head direction cells (9.1%; 6.1% pure, 3% mixed)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from functional classification of untagged cells.

claim: 18.9% of untagged cells were speed cells (10.1% pure, 8.8% mixed).
source: speed cells (18.9%; 10.1% pure, 8.8% mixed)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from functional classification of untagged cells.

claim: 5.8% of untagged cells were border cells (4.6% pure and 1.2% mixed).
source: border cells (5.8%; 4.6% pure and 1.2% mixed)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from functional classification of untagged cells.

claim: 41.6% of untagged cells were unclassified.
source: and unclassified cells (41.6%)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from functional classification of untagged cells.

claim: The untagged population had lower head direction scores compared to tagged cells (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 22869.0, p=0.003).
source: The untagged population had lower head direction scores (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 22869.0, p=0.003)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The untagged population had higher grid scores compared to tagged cells (Mann-Whitney U test, U = 14225.0, p=0.0037).
source: higher grid scores (Mann-Whitney U test, U = 14225.0, p=0.0037)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The untagged population had lower spatial information content compared to tagged cells (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 21692.0 p=0.036).
source: and lower spatial information content (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 21692.0 p=0.036) compared to the tagged cells
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no significant difference in border score between tagged and untagged populations (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 16536.0, p=0.085).
source: There was no significant difference in border score (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 16536.0, p=0.085)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no significant difference in speed score between tagged and untagged populations (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 18307.0, p=0.68).
source: or speed score (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 18307.0, p=0.68)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The classifier identified tagged cells as putative stellate cells 81.3% of the time.
source: We found that the classifier identified our tagged cells as putative stellate cells 81.3% of the time (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The extended dataset included 1332 cells including 411 grid cells.
source: We therefore evaluated their classifier on an extended dataset of 1332 cells including 411 grid cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the extended dataset.

claim: The extended dataset included recordings from the EC-tTA x tetO-ArchT-GFP mice and three additional mice with histologically confirmed layer II recordings (N = 270 putative pyramidal cells, 999 putative stellate and 63 cells in the guard zone).
source: This extended dataset included recordings from the EC-tTA x tetO-ArchT-GFP mice and three additional mice with histologically confirmed layer II recordings (N = 270 putative pyramidal cells, 999 putative stellate and 63 cells in the guard zone).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the extended dataset.

claim: The preferred firing phase of the cells was not evenly distributed across the theta cycle (Rayleigh test for non-uniformity, p=3.79 × 10−9).
source: The preferred firing phase of the cells was not evenly distributed across the theta cycle (Rayleigh test for non-uniformity, p=3.79 × 10−9)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were two peaks in the distribution of preferred firing phase: one near the peak and one near the trough of the oscillation.
source: and there were two peaks in the distribution: one near the peak and one near the trough of the oscillation (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2; see also [Newman and Hasselmo, 2014])
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cells classified as stellate cells had overall higher grid scores than cells that were classified as pyramidal cells (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 114913, p=0.0003).
source: In contrast to the Tang et al. findings, however, we found that cells classified as stellate cells had overall higher grid scores than cells that were classified as pyramidal cells (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 114913, p=0.0003).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: ~32% of the putative stellates were grid cells, compared to ~23% of the putative pyramidal cells.
source: Correspondingly,~32% of the putative stellates were grid cells, compared to ~23% of the putative pyramidal cells (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: There was no significant difference in border scores between putative stellate and putative pyramidal populations (two-sided Mann-Whitney U-Test, U = 127330.5, p=0.158).
source: We did not find a significant difference in border scores between the two populations (two-sided Mann-Whitney U-Test, U = 127330.5, p=0.158, Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Grid cells were significantly less theta modulated than non-grids (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 162644.0, p=9.28×10−5).
source: As a group, despite having many strongly modulated example cells, grid cells were significantly less theta modulated, as measured by the mean vector length of the cell firing with respect to the theta oscillation, than non-grids (Figure 4F; two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 162644.0, p=9.28×10−5)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The strength of theta modulation had a very weak but significant negative correlation to grid score (Pearson's r = −0.15, p=6×10−8).
source: Consistent with these results, the strength of theta modulation had a very weak but significant negative correlation to grid score (Pearson's r = −0.15, p=6×10−8; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Pure grid cells were not significantly different in theta modulation compared to pure border cells (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 22816, p=0.087).
source: Pure grid cells were not significantly different in theta modulation compared to pure border cells (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 22816, p=0.087, Figure 4G)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Pure grid cells had less theta modulation than pure speed cells (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 16548.0, p=0.0002).
source: but had less theta modulation than pure speed cells (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 16548.0, p=0.0002)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Pure grid cells had more theta modulation than pure head direction cells (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 23391.0, p=0.003).
source: and more theta modulation than pure head direction cells (two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, U = 23391.0, p=0.003)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Approximately one in four stellate cells are grid cells.
source: We have shown that stellate cells in layer II of the MEC can belong to multiple functional cell classes and that approximately one in four are grid cells.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data from optogenetic tagging.

claim: The relationship between the firing of the cell and the theta oscillation is a poor predictor of the functional identity of the cell.
source: These results show that, despite some differences between groups, the large diversity in theta modulation and preferred theta phase within cell types makes the relationship between the firing of the cell and the theta oscillation a poor predictor of the functional identity of the cell, in close agreement with the results of Latuske et al., 2015.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citation to Latuske et al., 2015.

claim: The actual proportion of grid cells among stellate cells may be larger than 25% due to spike sorting errors, boundary-induced distortions, and large inter-field spacing.
source: The actual proportion of grid cells may be larger than this estimate, for three reasons: (i) spike sorting errors can lead to misassignment of cells into the wrong functional class (Navratilova et al., 2016), (ii) boundary-induced distortions of the grid pattern could, in theory, cause a grid cell to fall below the cutoff (Stensola et al., 2015), and (iii) grid cells with inter-field spacing larger than our 0.8–1.0 meter recording box would be missed in our analysis (Stensola et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on known limitations of the methods, supported by citations.

claim: The majority of stellate cells are probably not grid cells.
source: Although the suggestion that one of four stellate cells probably is an underestimate, the majority of stellate cells are probably not grid cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing 25% of stellate cells are grid cells.

claim: PV+ cells are preferentially connected with grid cells in vivo.
source: On the one hand, PV+ cells are preferentially connected with grid cells in vivo (Buetfering et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Buetfering et al., 2014.

claim: Manipulations of the PV+ network alters grid cell firing.
source: and manipulations of the PV+ network alters grid cell firing (Fuchs et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fuchs et al., 2016.

claim: The effects of manipulating the PV+ network are not strictly limited to grid cells alone.
source: On the other hand, the effects of manipulating the PV+ network are not strictly limited to grid cells alone (Buetfering et al., 2014; Miao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buetfering et al., 2014 and Miao et al., 2017.

claim: Grid cells are likely present also among pyramidal cells, along with other functional cell types.
source: Moreover, although we cannot address the functional identity of layer II pyramidal cells using our approach due to the high numbers of non-expressing stellate cells, it is very likely that grid cells are present also among pyramidal cells, along with other functional cell types (Domnisoru et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Domnisoru et al., 2013 and Sun et al., 2015.

claim: There is no 1:1 relationship between morphological and functional cell types in layer II of the MEC.
source: Taken together, the observations suggest that there is no 1:1 relationship between morphological and functional cell types in layer II of the MEC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and observations.

claim: In vitro recordings have found some heterogeneity among both stellate cells and pyramidal cells.
source: In agreement with this possibility, in vitro recordings have found some heterogeneity among both stellate cells and pyramidal cells (Fuchs et al., 2016; Ferrante et al., 2017; Giocomo et al., 2007; Giocomo and Hasselmo, 2009; Shay et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In the visual cortex, a cell's morphology, projection pattern, and layer assignment does not define its functional class in a straightforward manner.
source: In the visual cortex, where there are also functionally defined cell types such as simple and complex cells, a cell's morphology, projection pattern, and layer assignment does not define its functional class in a straightforward manner (Gilbert and Wiesel, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gilbert and Wiesel, 1979.

claim: The diversity of functional cell types in the stellate population is consistent with the proposal that grid cells contribute to, but are not the sole determinant of, place cell firing.
source: The diversity of functional cell types in the stellate population is consistent with the proposal that grid cells contribute to, but are not the sole determinant of, place cell firing (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data, supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: Place cells show mature firing patterns before grid cells in development.
source: The observation fits with earlier results that place cells show mature firing patterns before grid cells in development (Langston et al., 2010; Wills et al., 2010; Bjerknes et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Langston et al., 2010; Wills et al., 2010; Bjerknes et al., 2018.

claim: Place cells can maintain some significant spatial tuning even when grid cells lose their hexagonal firing patterns.
source: and place cells can maintain some significant spatial tuning even when grid cells lose their hexagonal firing patterns (Brandon et al., 2011; Koenig et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Brandon et al., 2011 and Koenig et al., 2011.

claim: Border cells are present from the earliest days that place cells have been recorded in the hippocampus.
source: Such residual tuning could be upheld by border cells in MEC, which are present from the earliest days that place cells have been recorded in the hippocampus (Bjerknes et al., 2014; Muessig et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bjerknes et al., 2014 and Muessig et al., 2015.

claim: Border cells' spatial modulation is retained under circumstances that compromise the spatial periodicity of grid cells.
source: and whose spatial modulation is retained under circumstances that compromise the spatial periodicity of grid cells (Miao et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Miao et al., 2017.

claim: Stellate cells are required for path integration behaviors.
source: Taken together with recent work showing that stellate cells are required for path integration behaviors (Tennant et al., 2018), our data also implicate grid cells in path integration, in agreement with a large body of present and past theoretical models of grid cells (McNaughton et al., 2006; Couey et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tennant et al., 2018.

claim: The data implicate grid cells in path integration.
source: Taken together with recent work showing that stellate cells are required for path integration behaviors (Tennant et al., 2018), our data also implicate grid cells in path integration, in agreement with a large body of present and past theoretical models of grid cells (McNaughton et al., 2006; Couey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data combined with prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Roughly one in four of the tagged cells were grid cells.
source: Roughly one in four of the tagged cells were grid cells, suggesting that stellate cells contribute not only to path-integration-based representation of self-location but also have other functions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Stellate cells contribute not only to path-integration-based representation of self-location but also have other functions.
source: Roughly one in four of the tagged cells were grid cells, suggesting that stellate cells contribute not only to path-integration-based representation of self-location but also have other functions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that only 25% of stellate cells are grid cells.

claim: The data support observations suggesting that grid cells are not the sole determinant of place cell firing.
source: The data support observations suggesting that grid cells are not the sole determinant of place cell firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) is thought to create a map of space through a set of functionally distinct cell types: grid cells, border cells, head direction cells, and speed cells.
source: The medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) is thought to create a map of space through a set of functionally distinct cell types: grid cells, border cells, head direction cells, and speed cells (Rowland et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rowland et al., 2016.

claim: Each functional cell type in the MEC follows its own developmental trajectory.
source: Each functional cell type follows its own developmental trajectory (Bjerknes et al., 2014; Langston et al., 2010; Wills et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bjerknes et al., 2014; Langston et al., 2010; Wills et al., 2010.

claim: The functional identity of MEC cells is hardwired during development.
source: Each functional cell type follows its own developmental trajectory (Bjerknes et al., 2014; Langston et al., 2010; Wills et al., 2010), suggesting that the functional identity of the cell is hardwired during development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that cell types follow distinct developmental trajectories.

claim: Arch silences cells with near-zero latency.
source: Previous work has shown that Arch silences cells with near-zero latency (Chow et al., 2010; Wolff et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chow et al., 2010 and Wolff et al., 2014.

claim: Layer II grid cells phase-precess.
source: Individual grid cells showed large diversity in their preferred firing and depth of theta modulation (Figure 4B,E) as expected given the propensity of layer II grid cells to phase-precess (Hafting et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hafting et al., 2008.

claim: Grid cells are not homogeneously distributed in layer II.
source: As there are now clear indications from imaging work that grid cells are not homogeneously distributed in layer II (Heys et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Heys et al., 2014.
